planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in full sun and well-drained soil, allowing room for its large arching habit.

directions: This hybrid of Syringa josikaea and S. reflexa, raised by Isabella Preston in Canada, forms a large arching shrub topped with long, loosely drooping plumes of fragrant soft rosy-pink flowers about two weeks after common lilac finishes. Give it plenty of room to spread and avoid heavy pruning except to remove old or crossing wood, since the pendulous flower trusses are carried on arching branch tips. It holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit and tolerates a wide range of soils as long as drainage is adequate.

common_name: Mrs Edward Harding Lilac (Double Dark Pink French Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun.

directions: A 1920s Lemoine introduction, this French lilac opens deep claret-pink double buds that fade to a softer pink as the dense, conical panicles mature, giving a two-toned effect on the truss. Deadhead promptly after bloom since next year's flower buds set soon afterward, and thin a few of the oldest canes to ground level every few years to keep flowering on vigorous younger wood. It carries an RHS Award of Garden Merit and performs best where winters are cold enough to satisfy its dormancy needs.

common_name: Superba Littleleaf Lilac (Reblooming Fragrant Pink Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in full sun and well-drained, near-neutral soil; its fine twiggy habit suits smaller gardens better than common lilac.

directions: This littleleaf lilac selection bears loose, airy panicles of fragrant, single rosy-pink flowers in a heavy main flush in mid-spring, then often rewards gardeners with a lighter scattering of repeat blooms through summer and into fall. Its small leaves and twiggy, fine-textured habit stay more mildew-resistant through the season than most common-lilac types, and little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crowded stems after the main bloom. It has earned an RHS Award of Garden Merit and tolerates both drought and a range of soil types once established.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring or fall in full sun to light shade and moist, well-drained soil.

directions: A white-flowered selection of the species Hungarian lilac, Holger carries slender, elongated panicles of small, very fragrant tubular flowers from the latter half of May, well after common lilac has finished. Its upright, oval habit and dark green foliage that turns bronze to burgundy in fall make it useful as a tall screening shrub, and it tolerates heavier, moister soils better than most Syringa vulgaris cultivars. Little pruning is required beyond removing old or crowded wood after flowering.

common_name: Donald Wyman Preston Lilac (Late-Blooming Red-Purple Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in full sun; this extremely cold-hardy Preston hybrid tolerates far northern winters better than common lilac.

directions: Introduced in 1944 by hybridizer Frank Skinner of Dropmore, Manitoba, this Preston-group lilac opens purple buds to lightly fragrant red-purple single flowers carried in branching, pyramidal clusters at the stem tips. It blooms roughly a week to two weeks after common lilac, extending the lilac season into late spring, and its multi-stemmed, upright-spreading habit forms a large background shrub with little care beyond occasional removal of old canes. Extremely cold-hardy, it thrives where S. vulgaris cultivars often struggle.

common_name: Miss Canada Preston Lilac (Late-Blooming Rosy-Pink Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in full sun; extremely cold-hardy, it suits far-northern gardens where common lilac struggles.

directions: One of Isabella Preston's Ottawa-bred Syringa x prestoniae selections, Miss Canada opens violet-pink buds to brilliant, sweetly scented rosy-pink single flowers about a week later than common lilac, giving a second wave of lilac bloom in the garden. It grows into a dense, rounded, multi-stemmed shrub that can be left to form a large specimen or trained as a small tree, and needs only occasional removal of old wood to stay vigorous. It is reliably hardy even in Zone 2 winters.

common_name: James MacFarlane Preston Lilac (Late-Blooming Pink Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in full sun and well-drained to consistently moist soil.

directions: Introduced through the University of New Hampshire, this Preston-group lilac is smothered in lightly scented, true-pink single flowers roughly two weeks after common lilac blooms, making it one of the last lilacs to flower each season. Its large, crinkled, pointed leaves turn yellow in fall and the shrub tolerates wetter soil conditions that would be fatal to many Syringa vulgaris types. An upright, spreading, multi-stemmed habit needs only periodic thinning of old canes to stay full and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring or fall in full sun; this cold-hardy early lilac extends bloom ahead of common lilac by a week or more.

directions: Bred by Frank Skinner of Dropmore, Manitoba and introduced in 1935, Pocahontas opens deep maroon-purple buds into fragrant, deep violet single flowers roughly seven to ten days before common lilac varieties begin blooming, giving the earliest flush of lilac color in the garden. As one of the hardier hyacinthiflora hybrids, it forms a large, upright accent shrub that tolerates severe winters well beyond the limits of most Syringa vulgaris cultivars. Thin out old canes periodically to keep the shrub from becoming congested at the base.

common_name: Clarke's Giant Lilac (Large-Flowered Early Lavender-Blue Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring or fall in full sun to light shade and well-drained soil.

directions: Introduced by Clarke Nursery of San Jose, California in the early-to-mid 20th century, Clarke's Giant is prized for its unusually large clusters of fragrant, gentian blue-lavender single flowers that open well ahead of common lilac in early to mid spring. Its vigorous, medium-to-tall habit makes it a strong specimen or background shrub, and like other hyacinthiflora hybrids it sets flower buds quickly after bloom so pruning should follow soon after flowering ends. It performs reliably across a wide range of soils given full sun and good drainage.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in full sun; highly adaptable to both dry and moist sites once established.

directions: Bred by Frank Skinner in Dropmore, Manitoba and introduced in 1932, Asessippi produces an abundance of fragrant, single, pale lavender flowers in upright panicles that open well before common lilac, giving one of the earliest lilac displays of the season. Its large, multi-stemmed, upright-spreading form resists becoming leggy with age and adapts to a wide range of soil types and pH without complaint. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, making it a reliable choice for prairie and far-northern gardens.
